chapter_theme: Paripadal 10, the Vaigai: the flood announced by drums, the whole of Koodal going out to bathe, lovers' embraces and sulks, a tusker calming his frightened mate, love and toddy hidden from gossip, offerings and water-play, evening in the town, and the flood praised as giving like the Pandya.

paripadal:10:1-8.reading: When the rain has fallen on the mountain range in the evening and run on to join the sea whose bounds no one sees, easing the land's distress, the Vaigai's flood arrives, spreading its coarse sand like a many-folded coverlet, mixing tender striped mango shoots with plantain leaves, its sound beyond measure while drums are beaten to announce it.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet hails the river's coming as an event announced by drums: praise of the Vaigai (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the coarse sand the flood spreads over the bed

paripadal:10:1-8.nuance: The flood is given a herald: பறை அறைய in line 7 is the drum that tells the town the water has come, so the river enters the poem like a king entering a city. மாலை in line 1 may be 'evening' or 'the range' (the hills as a garland); the reading takes the hour.

paripadal:10:9-18.reading: To play in the flood the people crowd out, with fine threads tied at their feet and girdles of many strands pulled tight, carrying syringes of blood-red lac water and pearl-water paste, and they harness plumed horses swift as birds, she-elephants sweet to ride even when the water runs high, carts, mules, fine bullock carts and pole palanquins, and mount them in turn, hurrying in rows.

thinai_evidence.note: the crowd dresses and sets out for play in the river flood, the bathing of the watered-field land

comparisons.tenor: the horses, swift as birds
the rows of strands of the girdle
the lac dye in the water syringes

paripadal:10:9-18.nuance: The preparations are for a water-fight as much as a bath: நீரெக்கி (line 12) are squirts filled with red lac water, the festival weapon that returns in the play of lines 99 to 110.

paripadal:10:19-40.reading: Old and young, girls in the bud, new brides like flowers just opened, the rich, the dear ones, the half-grey and the white-haired, chaste wives, courtesans and companions all go from the town to the wide bank in a soft pace like music set to the drummers' beat, and there some watch the water, some ride the floats, some fight, ride horses or drive she-elephants, while near the flowered island some embrace the ones they love, some refuse the embrace and taste the honey of a sulk at night's end, and some, with love as the pick that breaks resistance, drop the screen and go to bed; and Koodal receives the flood we long for as women who escape their slow old guardians to meet their husbands, as men at a port receive the ship that reaches shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers' embrace and sulk at the river island, union in the watered land

comparisons.tenor: the girls not yet grown
the newly married young women

comparisons.vehicle: தாள விதி கூட்டிய இய மென் நடை
comparisons.tenor: the crowd's measured going to the river
the sulk that ends the night
love that breaks down resistance
Koodal receiving the Vaigai flood

paripadal:10:19-40.nuance: The list of bathers in line 23 sets பதிவத மாதர் and பரத்தையர் side by side, chaste wives and courtesans in one festival crowd, which the akam poems never do. The closing simile makes the whole city a lover: Koodal meets its flood as a wife meets the husband she has waited for.

paripadal:10:41-62.reading: A strong tusker sees a gentle she-elephant standing by an ornamented mansion, falls into longing and will not walk; she, going toward him with her heart on him, sees the tiger painted on the mansion wall, takes fright, ignores her driver and bolts while the women on her tremble, and the tusker shakes off his goad, trumpets like thunder, turns back, embraces her and twines his legs with hers, the beloved ending the beloved's fear like a pilot who knows the quarters mending with resin a ship whose sail and gear are giving way; then lovers whose fortified hearts the lute, song and dance have broken stand ashamed before the crowd, unable to choose, like two kings' armies that met and now stand joined, afraid to sound the cry of truce.

thinai_evidence.note: the beloved's fear ended by the beloved's embrace, shown in a pair of elephants

comparisons.tenor: the women walking with the she-elephant
the dark she-elephant

comparisons.vehicle: சிதையும் கலத்தைப் பயினான் திருத்தும் திசை அறி நீகானும்
comparisons.tenor: the tusker who steadies his terrified mate
the lovers held between shame before the crowd and desire

paripadal:10:41-62.nuance: This is not iraicchi in the brief's sense: line 52 states the sense outright (சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்) and two explicit similes follow, so the elephants are the subject and the deletion test fails. It is the akam elephant-pair image with its meaning spelled out. The fright is caused by a painted tiger, art mistaken for a beast. Lines 53 and 56 to 62 are compressed; what இதை, களிறு and பிணை name on the ship (sail and fittings) and who the shamed ones of lines 57 to 59 are is a reading.

paripadal:10:63-70.reading: As love surges and joy shows in the eyes, those who hide, fearing even the town's ruler, are like drinkers who guard their drunkenness: dreading gossip, hearts in turmoil, they suppress their high spirits while the world spreads talk, and so this flood brings toddy mixed with love that tears away the banks.

thinai_evidence.note: lovers who hide their union from the gossip of the crowd

comparisons.tenor: lovers who keep their love's excitement hidden
love and toddy that overflow restraint

paripadal:10:63-70.nuance: Love and toddy are joined twice, first as simile (the lover hides his joy as the drinker hides his drink) and then as the flood's own cargo (கள்ளொடு காமம் கலந்து). ஊர் மன்னும் (line 64) may be the town's king or simply 'the town' with a particle; the fear is in any case of being seen.

paripadal:10:71-88.reading: Tired from fighting the water, bathers leave their rafts; the smoke of burnt agil rises in the grove and the paste on women's breasts runs off like an opened sluice so that every quarter smells of it; some pour toddy from a cup uncovered like the moon slipping out of a cloud, and women with makara bands on their bright foreheads hold it in their palms like the full moon caught by the serpent and drink with lily mouths like celestial women drinking the moon; some wrap white silk, some twist their hair, some grind red saffron, agil and camphor into a paste red as sacrificial fire; some release snails, crabs, prawns and vaalai fish into the waves crying 'grow and flourish', and some, looking to what they lack, do good works in hope before they would ever speak the shame of asking.

thinai_evidence.note: toddy-drinking, fish and prawn of the river: the watered-field land's things

comparisons.tenor: the cup with its cover taken off
the cup held in the palm
the women drinking from the cup
the women's mouths
the red paste being ground

paripadal:10:71-88.nuance: Lines 85 to 88 are the rite inside the play: creatures are given back to the river with a blessing, and wishes are made by deeds instead of by asking, so that இளிவரவு, the humiliation the Kural attaches to begging, is kept out even of prayer. Several similes of lines 73 to 84 (the serpent-seized moon, the moon-drinking women, the oblation fire) are compressed and their exact tenors are a reading.

paripadal:10:89-98.reading: While bees hum with a curving voice like a cast bell, women steep cool red dyes and plunge into the water, knead ornament-dust to wash off oil, add garlands, sandal, musk and jewels to the water so that it is adorned, and feed the flood a toddy it cannot drink; the bright-bangled women's colour gleams, and after the bathing their eyes, streaked red, look like the file-sharpened tips of fine arrows, and so does the flower-eyed flood.

thinai_evidence.note: women bathing and pouring toddy into the river flood

comparisons.tenor: the curving hum of the bees

comparisons.vehicle: ஐ விரை மாண் பகழி அரம் தின் வாய்
comparisons.tenor: the women's eyes reddened by bathing
the flood strewn with flowers

paripadal:10:89-98.nuance: The bathers treat the river as a guest or a lover to be dressed and given drink: the water is garlanded, scented and offered toddy (உண்ணா நறவினை ஊட்டுவார்). Line 97 repeats போன்ம் three times and the sense of lines 95 to 98 is not secure.

paripadal:10:99-110.reading: Some push across with poles, some scatter the cool kandal pollen and the foam of the waves, some rest with rafts in the swift water, some swim slowly against the current, some take and eat the little flower-rice the soft girls cooked as the givers offer and refuse, slender girls snatch balls and kazhangu and run to leap from the bank, and young men clash with gleaming spears and swords, so that, like a field where elephants have fought, the sweet water of the flood is never clear, day after day.

thinai_evidence.note: play in the river: rafts, swimming and the girls' toy meals of the watered land

comparisons.tenor: the river churned by the bathers' play

paripadal:10:99-110.nuance: The simile turns the festival into a battle: the clear river is muddied as a war-field is trampled by elephants, and the young men's mock fight with weapons belongs to the same picture. The kandal is a seashore plant, out of place in the river scene.

paripadal:10:111-124.reading: When the evening wind under the moon sweeps the dark away, the people change their dress at the settling evening in Koodal, put off the day's ornaments and put on fresh garlands of opened flowers, armlets, earrings, bright jewels and pearls; there are singers' songs, praise and hymns, dancers' dances to the measured beat, and the fragrant honey and bees, all of it, as bees that follow the melody hum against it and bees settled in the hair hum in tune; and as you turn toward the south, the smoke from inside the gemmed mansions, mixed with pure scented water, rises with the turning wind like the mist that rises over the flowering creepers of a cold hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening the bathers return to Koodal, its music and incense

comparisons.vehicle: நளிர் மலைப் பூங்கொடித் தங்குபு உகக்கும் பனி வளர் ஆவி
comparisons.tenor: the smoke rising from the mansions of Koodal

paripadal:10:111-124.nuance: The poet turns to address the river (திரிதர்வாய், line 120) as it flows on south, so the town's evening is seen as what the river leaves behind. The closing simile brings a hill's mist into the city.

paripadal:10:125-130.reading: Like the Vazhuthi who pours gold until the outstretched hands of poets in want are full, the flood spreads its water and pours gold on the fields, and may that work never cease, says Koodal, which without strain feasts the flood that comes as a guest, while musicians and the household companions together praise it and bow.

thinai_evidence.note: the flood praised through the Pandya's giving and worshipped by Koodal

comparisons.vehicle: இலம்படு புலவர் ஏற்ற கை ஞெமரப் பொலம் சொரி வழுதி
comparisons.tenor: the flood spreading water over the fields

paripadal:10:125-130.nuance: The usual direction of Tamil praise is reversed: kings are likened to rain and river, but here the river is likened to the king, so the Pandya's giving is the fixed measure and nature is measured against it. The city treats the flood as a guest (விருந்து அயர் கூடல்). அருங் கறை in line 129 is obscure.

links.note: Akananuru 296's friend turns the hero away because he bathed in the great Vaigai with the dark girl (பெருநீர் வையை அவளொடு ஆடி) and the talk is like Koodal's clamour; Paripadal 10.19-23 lists chaste wives and courtesans (பதிவத மாதர், பரத்தையர்) going together to the Vaigai at Koodal.
links.teaches: Since the festival put wives and courtesans in the same flood openly, the friend's charge in Akananuru 296 cannot be the bathing itself, a licensed public pleasure, but the companion he chose, so the akam poem turns a shared civic rite into private evidence.

links.note: Kuruntokai 37's tusker strips yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger, left for the heroine to read as the hero's love; Paripadal 10.42-52 has a tusker turn back to embrace his terrified mate and says outright சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்.
links.teaches: The Paripadal poet spells out in one line the sense that Kuruntokai 37 leaves implied, which shows that the caring elephant pair was read by the poets themselves as an image of the lover who removes the beloved's distress.

links.note: Kural 1145 says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is craved each time one is drunk; Paripadal 10.63-68 likens lovers who hide their love from gossip to drinkers who hide their drunkenness.
links.teaches: Both join love and toddy, but the Kural's lover welcomes exposure while the Paripadal's festival lovers hide from it, so the same comparison serves to praise and to fear gossip, and the couplet's bravado reads as one stance among those the poets knew.

links.note: Akananuru 266's wife says her husband played in the evening flood with young women and lost his shame (நாண்இழந்து), and the talk is loud as a feast; Paripadal 10.63-68 shows lovers in the flood hiding their joy for fear of gossip (அலர் அஞ்சி).
links.teaches: The Paripadal shows that the flood-play crowd expected lovers to hide, so the wife's charge that he 'lost his shame' accuses him of breaking a restraint the festival itself kept, not of joining the play.

links.note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even water for a cow; Paripadal 10.87-88 has bathers who, seeing what they lack, do good works in hope before they speak the shame of asking (இளிவரவு கூறாமுன்).
links.teaches: The festival bathers apply the Kural's horror of asking even to what they want from the river, choosing an offering over a spoken request, so the ethic against begging shaped how people framed a petition in worship.

links.note: Kural 211 measures giving without return by the rain, to which the world gives nothing back; Paripadal 10.125-127 measures the Vaigai's flood over the fields by the Vazhuthi who pours gold into poets' hands.
links.teaches: The Kural makes nature the model for the giver, while the Paripadal makes the king the model for nature, so the pair shows the comparison between rain and royal giving could run in both directions, with the Pandya's gift treated as the surer standard.

links.note: Purananuru 3 counsels the Pandya Vazhuthi that suppliants have crossed deadly roads and his strength is to read their need and end their poverty; Paripadal 10.125-126 names the Vazhuthi who pours gold into the hands of poets in want (இலம்படு புலவர்).
links.teaches: What the puram poet urges on a Vazhuthi as a duty to be kept, the devotional poet takes as so settled a fact of the Pandya house that it can serve as the vehicle for praising the river itself.

source_issues: Paripadal 10: the core text has 130 lines but the source numbers its last line 131; printed line 100 stands on line 99 (flags).
Paripadal 10 line 9: flagged as a line once taken for a modern heading; it reads as verse (புனல் மண்டி ஆடல் புரிவான்) and is marked as such.
Paripadal 10 lines 28, 29, 42, 43, 44, 126, 129, 130 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 10 lines 69, 88 and 108: repaired from sangamtamil.com readings (flags).
Paripadal 10 line 97: போன்ம் is written three times (போன்ம் போன்ம் போன்ம்); possibly a copying repetition.
Paripadal 10: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.
